newsitem.title: GERMANY: Handelsblatt says Deutsche hit hard by funds.
newsitem.headline: Handelsblatt says Deutsche hit hard by funds.

text.p: A German business newspaper said that Deutsche Bank AG's German funds unit, DWS, will have to pay far more than previously expected as a result of severe problems at three of its British funds.

The Handelsblatt daily said in its Monday edition that Deutsche Bank reckons it will have to pay investors up to 230 million marks, while industry sources were quoted as saying the amount could reach 350 million marks.
A Deutsche Bank spokesman said he could not confirm the report.
Handelsblatt said that Deutsche Bank will probably also have to provide additional liquidity for the fund.
The 420 million marks that the bank has already transferred to London have already been used up because investors had sold investments worth 464 million marks before the weekend, the paper said.
Earlier on Sunday, Deutsche Bank said it did not expect to have to implement changes in its control mechanisms as a result of the problems at three of the bank's British funds.

In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Christian Strenger, spokesman for the management at DWS, said standards at DWS were already high and that investors were continuing to invest in the funds despite the U.K. problems.

Asked whether he expected the events at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management in London to have a negative impact on the German operation he said: "Definitely not, as German investors are well aware of the quality and solidity of German funds companies such as DWS."
"In case this needs confirmation -- even today we registered not insignificant purchases of DWS funds," he added.
Trading in three funds managed by MGAM, the Deutsche Bank group's British fund management unit, was temporarily halted this week due to "suspected irregularities".

The manager of two of the funds, Peter Young, was suspended and his personal assets frozen pending a probe into the management of the funds, which held a high proportion of unlisted, speculative high-technology stocks.
Worried investors sold off eight percent of the funds which were worth 1.14 billion pounds when they resumed trading on Thursday. A further five percent was sold on Friday.
Deutsche has pledged to tighten up its controlling mechanisms to prevent any recurrence.

Strenger denied that the German-based funds could be vulnerable to similar problems, adding that DWS would only invest in stocks without a full listing if it was clear that a listing was likely soon and that the company was sound.
"We examine such stocks particularly closely and using quality documents," he said.
He said there was no need for new, tighter controlling mechanisms, adding that standards were already being reviewed and improved all the time.

"The control systems which have been established and proven over 40 years are constantly being reviewed and reworked to build in new developments," he said. "This means our internal controls are guaranteed to be effective."
